US seasonal hiring is off to a weak start:

US-based employers announced plans to hire 90,787 workers in September, the weakest September total since 2011.

This marks a -23% decline from the 117,313 recorded in September 2025.

Retail led all industries last month, with 65,150 announced hires, followed by Aerospace and Defense at 5,300.

However, announced seasonal hiring is muted so far this year, with a combined 62,000 seasonal hires, compared with 100,800 announced by seasonal employers last September.

Year-to-date, US hiring plans have totaled 210,612 workers, the 2nd-lowest total for the first 9 months of the year in at least 10 years.

Retail leads all sectors with 66,557 announcements so far in 2026, followed by Technology, at 22,361, and Aerospace and Defense, at 21,841.

Hiring demand remains muted.

John Collison on why @Stripe calls January 1st, 2026 "day one of the singularity," and the record high of new companies being created:

"The Unix epoch is January 1st, 1970. We decided that the singularity epoch is January 1st, 2026... We are now in the singularity."

"It's not a total coincidence that we picked that date. It was the end of last year that I feel like for many of us it was the 'holy crap' moment when it came to coding models and how they're getting so good."

"All the AI folks talk about this idea of recursive self-improvement where the AI uses the AI to make itself better... People refer to the AI as this monolithic thing, but we are clearly in a world where AI capabilities are helping with the rate of improvement in AI."

"As a result of intelligence on tap getting much cheaper, new firm creation is way up. We're seeing the highest rates of new firm creation that we've seen in recent memory on Stripe, right now."

"Because when you have all these tools, it's easier to start a company, it's easier to actually make it successful."

"I think this technology has a lot to be optimistic about. And so we don't see the singularity in any kind of a pessimistic or worried manner. We are in this moment of AI takeoff right now."

@collision w/ @mollyoshea

.@heronpower CEO Drew Baglino on the 40-year streak that kept US electricity flat while the economy grew, and why it just ended:

"We benefited from energy efficiency from the '70s... until like the 2010s. You saw efficiency everywhere... And all of that energy efficiency more or less negated the growth in energy services."

"The energy services were growing over time in the United States, but the net electricity delivered to accomplish those energy services stayed basically flat. And the same thing even happened in data centers."

"If you look at the efficiency of compute, even with all the AI things that are going on, in terms of flops per watt, it's really gone up an immense amount from the first data centers to today."

"And that has allowed more and more compute capability for the same percentage of GDP electricity production."

"Now it's changing... We are seeing electricity growth higher than it's ever been before. And that's not just because the benefits of energy efficiency are tailing off, it's because we are seeing broad based demand for more electricity: compute, transportation, industrial electrification."

"Electricity as a carrier is incredibly flexible... whether it's for intelligence or for heating, I see it as a great thing and wanna accelerate it."

@baglino @heronpower

The gap between AI names and the rest of the market is historic:

Since the start of 2024, a basket of 42 AI stocks has generated 67% of the S&P 500's price return.

In other words, those names have contributed +22 percentage points to the index’s +33% gain over this period.

By comparison, the remaining 458 stocks have added +11 percentage points.

Additionally, those 42 AI stocks have accounted for 58% of the S&P 500's earnings growth and 81% of CapEx and R&D growth since the start of 2024.

The rest of the index has therefore contributed just 20% of total CapEx and R&D growth over the same period.

Meanwhile, just 29% of stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 over the last 3 years, close to the ~25% low recorded during the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble.

AI is all that matters.

Dmitri Dolgov of @Waymo on how to tell if you’re one year away from shipping or ten:

"One pattern that I've seen over and over again is do you have convergence of discovery? The problems that you are seeing today, how different are they from the problems you saw six months ago?"

"As you're pushing on the system, does it feel like you have stability, and you're just iteratively improving your metrics in the same areas?"

"Or does it feel like every six months the landscape is shifting from under you and the problems of today are very different from what you saw a while ago?

"If you don't have that stability, then that's often a good indicator that you got some ways to go."

"If you think you're six months or a year away from deployment, do you have a scorecard that if it were green today would allow you to deploy with confidence?"

"If you don't have one, you're saving that for later, often that turns out to be more difficult than you expected, and there's a long distance to go."

"But if you already have one and you're seeing stability in your discovery and stability in your metrics, and it's just a matter of closing the gap, that is a really good indicator that you're getting pretty close."

@dmitri_dolgov w/ South Park Commons

US families are falling behind on debt payments.

The percentage of families reporting overdue loan payments surged to 19.6% in 2025, the highest since 2010, according to the Fed data.

This marks a sharp increase from 12.2% recorded in 2022.

This also reverses the gradual improvement between 2013 and 2019, when the percentage declined by -2.6 points.

Furthermore, more than 8.0% of families reported they were at least 2 months behind on payments, up from 5.0% in 2022.

This comes despite the typical family debt load remaining unchanged since 2022, suggesting that more households are struggling to keep up with existing financial obligations.

Americans are falling behind on loan payments at a concerning pace.

Airbnb's Brian Chesky on the classic management philosophy, and why he rejects it:

"Go through the list of great CEOs, almost none of them that I'm aware of do recurring one-on-ones... Jensen Huang does not do recurring one-on-ones, famously."

"I do think a CEO should meet one-on-one with your people. I don't think it should be recurring... If you wanna get time with me, get a meeting with me. If you wanna call me, call me. Bump into me, talk to me. But most of my recurring meetings are group meetings."

"If there's lots of one-way kinda sensitive topics, there's probably something wrong in the company... If we're having all these sensitive conversations, well, why are they so sensitive? Why can't other people hear about them?"

"If I have a one-on-one with you and you tell me there's a problem and we debate it and we say, 'Here's the solution,' we haven't consulted anyone else. So now we just made a decision and no one else helped, consulted, or knew how we made that decision."

"'Hire great people, trust them, let them do their job, stay out of the details, do recurring one-on-ones.' I don't believe any of that, and I wanna acknowledge that many great leaders do."

@bchesky w/ @sampjacobs

Rich on paper, dependent in practice. A trade developed world has made without noticing.

🌎🚨 Bond markets are starting to do central banks' job for them as investors have priced out nearly 180 basis points of expected rate hikes across eight major economies.

📉 Rising bond yields are tightening financial conditions without central banks having to intervene. Households face higher borrowing costs, companies have to finance their investments at less favorable rates, and governments are gradually seeing their refinancing costs increase. All of this weighs on economic activity and could therefore reduce the need for central banks to raise policy rates further. The cumulative rate hikes expected over the next 12 months across eight economies have fallen from 717 to 539 basis points since September.

⚠️ However, not all increases in long-term yields are created equal. If yields are rising because the economy is strong or investors expect persistent inflation, that's one thing, but if they're rising because markets are demanding higher risk premiums to finance government deficits, that's a different story. Right now, we're dealing with a combination of both. Between massive US deficits, concerns over France's public finances, enormous AI-related financing needs and the energy shock triggered by the conflict with Iran, the pressure on long-term yields goes well beyond monetary policy. I believe the risk is that central banks stop raising rates, or even start cutting them, without financial conditions actually improving.

➡️ There is another thing that I believe is fundamental. If long-term yields keep climbing despite policy rates stabilizing, we could see renewed discussions around slowing QT, Operation Twist-style interventions, or outright bond purchases. None of this is inevitable or necessarily desirable as intervening to suppress yields while inflation remains elevated could undermine monetary credibility and fuel even higher risk premiums.

For years, markets were mainly worried about central banks tightening financial conditions too aggressively, but now the risk is that they may no longer be able to ease financial conditions sufficiently, even when they want to.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/iV58Caf7pk

Active bond managers sell the dream of beating the index. Almost none of them do.

Over the past 10 years, nearly every category of active fixed income fund trailed its benchmark. Government intermediate funds: 100% underperformed. General government: 96%.

The edge top managers once had is gone too. The best-worst spread collapsed from 1.9% a year in the 2000s to 1.1% since 2020, per Apollo.

Public core fixed income is beta you are paying active fees for. Index it.
